Unit 1: Introduction to Accounting — The Language of Business & Economic Architecture

Term 1, AY 2026–2027 • Course Architect & Instructor: Prof. Filbert Richerd N. Ng Tsai

Section 1.1

The Practical Reality of Business: Why Accounting Matters to Everyone

Foundational Literacy
📌 TLDR — Section 1.1
You cannot operate, evaluate, or invest in a business without understanding accounting. Accounting is not just for CPAs; it is the universal scorecard that tells managers if their strategy is viable, warns founders when cash is running out, and demonstrates to banks and investors that an enterprise can service its debts.

1.1.1 The Scorecard of Economic Activity

Imagine watching a competitive UAAP basketball game where nobody keeps score, the referee has no whistle, fouls are not tracked, and the shot clock does not run. Players might exert tremendous energy running up and down the court, but nobody—neither the team owners, the head coach, the players, nor the fans—would have any objective way of knowing who is winning, who is playing efficiently, or how substitutions should be made.

In the commercial world, accounting is that official scorecard. Every single day, a commercial enterprise executes hundreds or thousands of disparate physical acts:

  • Baristas steam milk and serve lattes at a Taft Avenue cafe.
  • Programmers write lines of code for a cloud software startup in Bonifacio Global City.
  • Delivery drivers transport parcels across Metro Manila.
  • Human resource managers interview prospective sales managers.

None of these physical activities inherently look like numbers. However, to understand whether the enterprise is surviving, expanding, or heading toward bankruptcy, every single operational action must be translated into a common, objective denominator. That common denominator is money (Php ), and the system that systematically tracks, measures, and communicates this transformation is accounting.

1.1.2 Why Non-Accountants Must Understand Accounting

A dangerous misconception held by many first-year university students is: "I am majoring in Marketing, Finance, Entrepreneurship, or Management, so I don't need to know accounting; I will simply hire an accountant to handle the numbers." In corporate reality, this mindset is fatal:

The Marketing Executive

Designs a stunning Php 3,000,000 viral ad campaign generating 50% more foot traffic. But without understanding unit cost of goods sold (COGS) and contribution margin, each item is sold at an operational loss. More sales simply burn cash faster!

The Tech Entrepreneur

Raises Php 10,000,000 in seed capital for an app. Focuses entirely on user acquisition while ignoring monthly cash burn rate and accounts payable schedules. In 9 months, cash hits zero and payroll bounces.

The Commercial Banker

Reviews a Php 50,000,000 loan request. If the credit analyst cannot dissect debt-to-equity ratios, interest coverage, and operating cash flows, the bank risks lending depositors' money to an insolvent borrower.

Section 1.2

The Language of Business & The Translation Engine

Universal Vocabulary
📌 TLDR — Section 1.2
Accounting provides the standardized vocabulary that allows diverse stakeholders (investors, managers, creditors, tax authorities) across the globe to communicate economic health and operational performance without ambiguity.

Business relies on structured, universally recognized accounting vocabulary standardized under Philippine Financial Reporting Standards (PFRS) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS):

  • Assets: Economic resources controlled by the entity resulting from past events that will generate future economic benefits (cash, receivables, inventory, machinery).
  • Liabilities: Present legal or constructive obligations to transfer economic resources to other parties resulting from past transactions (bank loans, trade payables, accrued taxes).
  • Owner's Equity: The residual interest in the assets of the enterprise after deducting all liabilities (Assets − Liabilities).
  • Working Capital: Operating liquidity available for daily business (Current Assets − Current Liabilities).
  • Gross Profit Margin: The percentage of revenue remaining after subtracting direct costs of goods sold (Sales − COGSSales).
Section 1.3

The Interdisciplinary Matrix: Accounting, Economics, Finance, and MIS

The Business Matrix
📌 TLDR — Section 1.3
Accounting serves as the verifiable historical and current factual baseline. Economics provides theoretical market models and opportunity cost concepts; Finance takes accounting reports to forecast future value and allocate capital; Management Information Systems (MIS) automates and pipes accounting data in real time across the enterprise.

1.3.1 Accounting vs. Economics

Economics studies how societies allocate scarce resources, analyzing inflation, consumer elasticity, and Opportunity Cost (the value of the best alternative forgone). Accounting is empirical and transaction-driven, recording transactions strictly based on verifiable, historical cash and contractual exchanges.

💡 Sofia's Bakery Dilemma: Accounting Profit vs. Economic Profit

Sofia resigns from her corporate banking job (salary: Php 1,200,000/yr) and uses Php 2,000,000 of personal savings (which earned Php 100,000 annual interest) to open a bakery. In Year 1, her sales are Php 4,500,000 and explicit operating expenses are Php 3,800,000.

• Accounting View: Net Profit = Php 4,500,000 − Php 3,800,000 = +Php 700,000 (Profitable; pays income tax on Php 700k).

• Economic View: Opportunity Costs = Php 1,200,000 (salary) + Php 100,000 (interest) = Php 1,300,000.
Economic Profit = Php 700,000 − Php 1,300,000 = −Php 600,000! Economically, Sofia is Php 600k worse off than staying in banking. Both views are vital!

1.3.2 Accounting vs. Finance

Accounting looks at the past and present to build accurate, audited scorecards. Finance looks to the future, taking accounting statements as empirical data to project multi-year cash flow forecasts, calculate cost of capital, and price company shares.

The "Capital" Divergence: In Accounting, Capital refers strictly to Owner's Equity (net worth: Assets - Liabilities). In Finance, Capital refers to Total Invested Capital (Debt Capital + Equity Capital), evaluating asset financing under the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).

1.3.3 Role of Management Information Systems (MIS) and ERPs

Modern accounting is embedded in computerized ERPs like SAP S/4HANA and Oracle NetSuite. When a customer buys a Chickenjoy meal at Jollibee with GCash, the ERP simultaneously debits Cash/Receivable, credits Sales Revenue & VAT, debits COGS and credits Inventory, deducts the chicken piece from the commissary, and recalculates nationwide sales on the CFO's live dashboard!

Section 1.4

Financial Data vs. Non-Financial Information: What the Balance Sheet Captures (and What it Misses)

Strategic Indicators
📌 TLDR — Section 1.4
Accounting records only transactions quantifiable in monetary terms. While financial metrics reveal historical solvency and margins, modern enterprise valuation requires tracking non-financial operational drivers (customer satisfaction, employee turnover, carbon emissions, cybersecurity) that dictate future survival.
Financial Data (Captured on General Ledger)Non-Financial Information (Captured in MIS & ESG)
Cash in bank and marketable securitiesCustomer Satisfaction (CSAT / Net Promoter Score)
Accounts Receivable & aging schedulesEmployee Turnover Rate & Engineering Morale
Merchandise Inventory carrying valuesCarbon Footprint & Environmental Sustainability
Historical cost of buildings & equipmentDefect Rates, Delivery Lead Times & Return Rates
Net Income, Gross Margin & EBITDACybersecurity Resilience & Brand Reputation
💡 The Kodak Case Vignette: Why Non-Financial Indicators Dictate Survival

In 1996, Eastman Kodak was the global king of photography, generating over USD 16 Billion in revenue and over USD 1 Billion in accounting profits selling chemical film. However, non-financial MIS data showed customer sentiment moving rapidly to digital photography, and competitors filing thousands of digital sensor patents. Because balance sheets could not place a dollar value on digital disruption, Kodak failed to adapt and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

Section 1.5

Reporting Motivations & Strategic Biases: Public vs. Private Companies

Incentives Analysis
📌 TLDR — Section 1.5
Accounting records are not neutral physical laws; they are prepared by human managers with distinct incentives. Publicly listed firms face intense pressure to overstate revenues and delay expenses to boost stock prices; private firms face incentives to minimize reported profits to lower BIR income taxes. Independent audits exist to restore reliability.
🏢 Public Companies: Upward Bias (Profit Maximization)

Scrutinized by stock market analysts and shareholders who reward quarterly Earnings Per Share (EPS) growth. Driven by executive stock option bonuses. Common biases include aggressive premature revenue recognition, improperly capitalizing operating costs into assets, and understating bad debt provisions.

🏠 Private Businesses: Downward Bias (Tax Minimization)

Owned by families or small groups. Driven by legally minimizing annual corporate income tax (20%-25%) paid to the BIR under the CREATE Law. Common biases include accelerating depreciation write-offs, expensing equipment immediately, and deferring sales invoices to future tax periods.

🏛️ Departmental Exam Flashpoint: Non-Cash Asset Investments & Debt Assumption Traps

Across AY 2025–2026 departmental quizzes (Term 1 Q11, Term 2 Q5, Term 3 Q1 & Q11), examiners repeatedly test two foundational rules regarding owner capital contributions:

Rule 1: Fair Market Value (FMV) Over Historical Cost

When an owner transfers non-cash personal assets (e.g., machinery, delivery vehicles, computers) into the business, they are recorded at their Fair Market Value at the investment date. The owner's historical original purchase price is completely irrelevant to the business books.

• Example: Van bought for Php 1,000,000 with FMV Php 850,000 → Record Vehicle & Capital at Php 850,000.
Rule 2: Debt Assumption on Capital Contributions

If an invested asset has an unpaid liability that the business agrees to assume, the owner's capital credit is strictly the net equity contribution (Asset FMV − Assumed Debt).

• Example: Computer Php 50,000 with Php 40,000 debt assumed + Cash Php 100,000 → Capital Credit = Php 100,000 + (Php 50,000 − Php 40,000) = Php 110,000.
Section 1.6

The Principal-Agent Conflict & Corporate Governance (Agency Theory)

Governance & Audits
📌 TLDR — Section 1.6
When business owners (Principals) hire professional managers (Agents) to run their company, conflicting personal goals and information asymmetry create moral hazard. Standardized accounting rules, internal controls, and independent CPA audits are the vital governance tools that protect owners' capital.

In modern corporations like Ayala or San Miguel, ownership is dispersed among thousands of public stockholders (Principals). They elect a Board of Directors who hire executives (Agents) to manage operations. Managers possess inside information (information asymmetry), creating moral hazard—managers may be tempted to consume excessive perks or slash long-term research to hit short-term bonus targets.

Accounting mitigates agency costs through: (1) strict PFRS uniform measurement rules, (2) internal controls & segregation of duties, and (3) mandatory independent external audits conducted by CPA firms (SGV, PwC, KPMG, Deloitte).

Section 1.7

Streamlined Origins: From Clay Tokens to Fra Luca Pacioli

Practical Heritage
📌 TLDR — Section 1.7
Accounting was not invented in a classroom; it evolved over thousands of years as an essential practical tool for trade and tax enforcement. Fra Luca Pacioli did not invent double-entry bookkeeping, but he was the first to organize, standardize, and publish the Venetian system in 1494, earning him the title "Father of Modern Accounting."
🏺 Mesopotamia (3500 BCE)

Clay tokens in hollow spheres (bullae) tracked grain taxes. Scribes impressed token shapes onto wet clay, inventing cuneiform writing specifically to record accounting ledgers.

📜 Ancient Egypt (3000 BCE)

Pharaohs' granaries employed two independent scribes to record the exact same grain deliveries on separate papyrus rolls—the world's first dual-control segregation of duties.

📖 Venice (1494 CE)

Franciscan friar Fra Luca Pacioli published Summa de Arithmetica containing "Particularis de Computis et Scripturis", organizing and publishing double-entry bookkeeping across Europe.

Section 1.8

Definition, Nature, and the 4 Operational Phases of Accounting

AICPA Standard
📌 TLDR — Section 1.8
Under the 1953 AICPA definition, accounting is an art of 4 sequential phases: Recording (journalizing raw transactions), Classifying (posting to ledger accounts), Summarizing (building formal financial statements), and Interpreting (analyzing ratios and performance to make strategic decisions).
PhaseTool / BookCore FunctionApplication in Luna Creative Studio
1. RecordingGeneral JournalChronological entry of transactions based on source documents.Debiting Cash Php 60,000; Crediting Service Revenue Php 60,000 based on Official Receipt #101.
2. ClassifyingGeneral Ledger / T-AccountsSorting journal entries into individual account ledgers.Posting the debit into Cash (Account #101) and credit to Service Revenue (Account #401).
3. SummarizingFinancial StatementsAggregating ledger balances into formal periodic reports.Preparing Statement of Profit or Loss showing Php 220,000 revenues and Php 115,000 expenses.
4. InterpretingRatio AnalysisAnalyzing trends to make informed business decisions.Calculating Net Profit Margin (47.7%) to decide whether to hire an assistant designer.
Section 1.9

Areas of Practice & Specialized Branches of Accounting

Career Sectors
📌 TLDR — Section 1.9
Accountants practice across three major employment domains: Public Accounting (independent CPA firms providing audit/tax/MAS), Private Accounting (working as internal employees of a commercial business), and Government Accounting (custodians of public funds under COA, BIR, and DBM).
🏢 Public Accounting

External auditing, tax advisory, and management consulting (MAS) offered to clients for professional fees (SGV, PwC, KPMG, Deloitte).

🏭 Private Accounting

Employed directly within a commercial firm as Controller, CFO, Internal Auditor, or Cost Accountant (Jollibee, San Miguel, Ayala).

🏛️ Government Accounting

Administering and auditing public funds under the Commission on Audit (COA), BIR, and DBM in compliance with the Government Accounting Manual.

Section 1.10

Users of Accounting Information (IFRS Conceptual Framework 1.5)

Stakeholder Framework
📌 TLDR — Section 1.10
Under Section 1.5 of the IFRS Conceptual Framework, Primary Users are existing and prospective investors, lenders, and trade creditors who must rely on general-purpose financial reports because they lack the legal power to demand custom reports directly from management.
⭐ Primary Users (Conceptual Framework 1.5)
  • Investors: Assess profitability, risk/return, and buy/hold/sell decisions.
  • Lenders (Banks): Evaluate cash flows to ensure timely debt and interest repayments.
  • Trade Creditors: Determine credit limits and payment terms (e.g., 2/10, n/30).
🌐 Other Users
  • Management: Internal operational resource allocation and pricing.
  • Tax Authorities (BIR): Assess income, VAT, and local business taxes.
  • Employees & Labor Unions: Wage negotiations, bonuses, and stability.
Section 1.11

Forms of Business Organization in the Philippine Legal Framework

Statutory Structure
📌 TLDR — Section 1.11
Philippine commerce operates under three primary legal structures: Sole Proprietorships (1 owner, unlimited personal liability), Partnerships (2+ partners, separate legal entity, unlimited liability for general partners under Civil Code Art. 1767), and Corporations (separate legal person, limited liability, perpetual life under RA 11232). Regulated professions (CPAs, doctors, lawyers) cannot incorporate.
DimensionSole ProprietorshipPartnership (RA 386)Corporation (RA 11232)
OwnershipExactly 1 Individual2 or more Partners1 or more Stockholders (OPC allowed)
Juridical PersonalityNone (Owner & firm identical)Has separate legal personalitySeparate legal entity created by law
Owner's LiabilityUnlimited (Personal assets liable)Unlimited (General partners liable)Limited (To share investment)
Business LifeLimited (Ends on death/choice)Limited (Dissolves on partner death)Perpetual Existence
⚠️ Regulated Professions in the Philippines

Practicing professionals (CPAs, Doctors, Lawyers, Architects) cannot incorporate because limited liability would shield them from personal malpractice claims. They must practice as Sole Proprietors or form General Professional Partnerships (GPP).

Section 1.12

Artificial Intelligence and the Evolution of the Accounting Profession

Digital Frontier
📌 TLDR — Section 1.12
AI is rapidly automating repetitive, rule-based bookkeeping tasks (data entry, receipt scanning, invoice matching, bank reconciliation). However, AI cannot replace human professional judgment, ethical discernment, forensic investigation, or strategic executive advisory. Accountants who leverage AI will replace those who do not.
🤖 What AI Automates

OCR receipt capture, automated 3-way invoice matching in ERPs, automated bank reconciliations, 24/7 anomaly and duplicate ledger transaction detection.

🧠 What Human CPAs Deliver

Subjective revenue recognition contract interpretation, strategic tax planning, uncovering executive fraud and collusive bribery, and advising boards on M&A and capital structure.

Section 1.13

Unit 1 Comprehensive Assessment Battery (25 Questions & Solutions)

Master Self-Study Bank

Test your conceptual understanding. Click "Reveal Detailed Solution & Rationale" on any question to inspect the complete explanation.

Practice Case 1 • Business Form & Liability

Scenario: Marco has Php 3,000,000 in savings and a family home valued at Php 12,000,000. He and two partners want to start "SpeedyTransit Logistics." If structured as a General Partnership, is Marco's home protected from lawsuits if a delivery truck causes an accident? What legal structure protects him?

Solution & Legal Basis:
1. No, his home is NOT protected in a General Partnership. Under Article 1816 of the Philippine Civil Code (RA 386), all partners in a general partnership are liable pro rata with all their personal property for partnership debts after partnership assets are exhausted.
2. They should form a Corporation under RA 11232. A corporation possesses a distinct legal personality (Sec. 2). Stockholders enjoy the doctrine of limited liability; their liability is strictly capped at their invested capital, shielding Marco's personal home.
Practice Case 2 • Accounting vs Economic Profit

Scenario: Dr. Julian leaves a Php 1,800,000/yr hospital job and liquidates Php 2,500,000 in bonds paying 6% annual interest to open a clinic. In Year 1, clinic revenues are Php 4,800,000 and operating expenses are Php 2,800,000. Calculate (1) Accounting Net Profit, (2) Opportunity Costs, and (3) Economic Profit.

Step-by-Step Mathematical Solution:
1. Accounting Net Profit: Revenues (Php 4,800,000) − Expenses (Php 2,800,000) = +Php 2,000,000.
2. Opportunity Costs: Forgone salary (Php 1,800,000) + Forgone bond interest (Php 2,500,000 × 6% = Php 150,000) = Php 1,950,000.
3. Economic Profit: Accounting Profit (Php 2,000,000) − Opportunity Costs (Php 1,950,000) = +Php 50,000. Decision was economically sound!
Practice Case 3 • Reporting Bias Analysis

Scenario: Public Company A and Private Family Company B each spend Php 2,000,000 cash on an equipment overhaul extending useful life by 5 years. How is Company A motivated to treat this? How is Company B motivated to treat this? Why?

Strategic Rationale:
• Company A will CAPITALIZE the Php 2,000,000 as an Asset Improvement, spreading the cost over 5 years of depreciation (Php 400,000/yr). This inflates current-year net income by Php 1,600,000, boosting its stock price and executive bonuses.
• Company B will EXPENSE the entire Php 2,000,000 immediately as Repairs Expense, lowering taxable net income by Php 2,000,000 and saving Php 500,000 in cash taxes paid to the BIR (assuming a 25% tax rate).
Textbook Chapter 2

Unit 2: Accounting Concepts, Principles & Underlying Assumptions — The Conceptual Architecture

Term 1, AY 2026–2027 • Course Architect & Instructor: Prof. Filbert Richerd N. Ng Tsai

Section 2.1

Why Rules Matter: The Architectural Foundation of Accounting

Ground Rules
📌 TLDR — Section 2.1
Commerce is continuous and chaotic. Without standardized accounting rules and underlying assumptions, financial statements would be subjective works of fiction. The IFRS Conceptual Framework establishes the universal ground rules that ensure numbers prepared by different companies are comparable, verifiable, and trustworthy.

Imagine walking into a supermarket where every vendor invents their own definition of a "kilogram." One meatpacker labels a 200g cut as "1 kg" because they measured the cow when it was alive; another calls 500g "1 kg" because they measured it in dry desert air. As a consumer, you could never determine how much you are buying, and commerce would collapse.

In corporate reality, this exact disaster occurs without Philippine Financial Reporting Standards (PFRS) and the IFRS Conceptual Framework. If real estate developers could invent their own definition of "Revenue," they might book Php 500,000,000 the moment a buyer visits an open house. If airlines invented their own rules for "Expense," they might defer recording jet fuel costs for 10 years until the aircraft retires!

Standard accounting concepts and principles are not academic trivia; they are the hard-won structural architecture of global capitalism designed to protect investors, creditors, and the public from corporate deception.

Section 2.2

The Five Underlying Assumptions (Intuitive Guide for College Beginners)

Foundational Pillars
📌 TLDR — Section 2.2
The five accounting assumptions are foundational premises that make financial reporting possible: 1. Separate Entity ("Two Pockets" Rule): The firm is distinct from its owners. Personal spending must never enter business books. 2. Going Concern ("Train on Tracks" Rule): Assumes indefinite operation, justifying historical cost less depreciation instead of liquidation fire-sale values. 3. Monetary Unit ("Stable Yardstick" Rule): Quantifies events in Php , assuming stable purchasing power while ignoring unquantifiable intangibles. 4. Time Period ("Calendar Slice" Rule): Divides continuous life into artificial intervals (months, quarters, years) for timely performance checks. 5. Accrual Basis ("Earned vs. Incurred" Rule): Records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash flow timing.

2.2.1 The Business Entity / Separate Entity Assumption (The "Two Pockets" Rule)

The economic activities of an enterprise are strictly separate and distinct from the personal affairs of its owners, managers, or any other commercial entity.

💡 Real-World Scenario: Christian's Taft Specialty Burgers

Christian opens a burger cafe along Taft Avenue as a sole proprietorship. On Friday night, Christian withdraws Php 15,000 in cash directly from the burger shop's cash register to buy Coldplay VIP concert tickets for himself and his friends.

• Novice Bookkeeper Mistake: Debits "Entertainment Expense" of the cafe. This is a severe accounting violation! The concert tickets did not flip burgers, pay grill cooks, or keep lights on; they were purely personal luxuries.

• Correct Accounting: Debit Christian, Drawings (Capital Distribution) and Credit Cash. The withdrawal represents Christian taking back invested capital, directly reducing Owner's Equity.

Legal vs. Accounting Reality: Even though a sole proprietor has unlimited legal liability for commercial debts under civil law, for accounting and bookkeeping purposes, the business entity assumption is absolute.

2.2.2 The Going Concern Assumption (The "Train on the Tracks" Rule)

Accounting assumes that the business enterprise will continue operating indefinitely into the foreseeable future and has neither the intention nor the necessity to liquidate or drastically curtail operations.

If an enterprise were liquidating tomorrow, its commercial ovens, laptops, and delivery vans would only fetch 10 to 20 centavos on the peso at a liquidation pawnshop auction. Because we assume the business is a going concern, we do not write down assets to liquidation values. Instead, we record them at Historical Cost and systematically amortize them over their useful economic lives as Depreciation Expense.

When Going Concern Breaks: If an independent auditor discovers impending debt default or regulatory shutdown, an adverse going-concern audit warning is issued. The firm is forced to abandon PFRS and prepare financial statements on a Liquidation Basis—slashing all assets to immediate cash fire-sale values.

2.2.3 The Monetary Unit Assumption (The "Stable Yardstick" Rule)

The Monetary Unit assumption encompasses two core dimensions:

  • Unit of Measure (Quantification): Money is the common denominator of commercial activity. Only transactions that can be stated in terms of currency (Philippine Peso Php ) are recorded. You cannot list "10 laptops, 5 motorcycles, and 3 friendly baristas" on a balance sheet; they must be quantified in pesos.
  • Stable Currency Assumption: Assumes that the purchasing power of the monetary unit remains relatively stable over time. Standard accounting ignores general economic inflation for ordinary financial reporting (unless hyperinflation exceeds 100% over three years under PAS 29).
⚠️ Inherent Limitation of the Monetary Unit

Crucial competitive advantages cannot appear as assets on the balance sheet: stellar brand loyalty, employee workplace morale, and executive genius are omitted because no verifiable peso invoice exists for them.

2.2.4 The Time Period / Periodicity Assumption (The "Calendar Slice" Rule)

While an enterprise operates continuously, its indefinite operating life is artificially subdivided into equal, discrete time intervals (Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-Annually, or Annually) to provide timely financial reports.

  • Calendar Year: A 12-month period beginning January 1 and ending December 31.
  • Fiscal Year: Any 12-month consecutive accounting period chosen by an entity (e.g., July 1 to June 30, commonly chosen by agricultural firms matching crop harvest cycles or retailers ending in January after holiday returns).
  • Interim Periods: Accounting periods shorter than one full year (e.g., Quarterly SEC Form 17-Q reports).

2.2.5 The Accrual Basis of Accounting (The "Earned vs. Incurred" Rule)

PFRS Accrual Mandate
REVENUES: Recognized when EARNED (Goods delivered or services rendered), regardless of when cash is collected.
EXPENSES: Recognized when INCURRED (Assets consumed or services utilized), regardless of when cash is paid.

Why Cash Basis is Banned under PFRS: Cash accounting distorts operational reality. A construction company could spend Php 50,000,000 building a university facility in 2026, but if the client settles in January 2027, cash accounting would show a catastrophic Php 50M loss in 2026 and an artificial Php 70M profit in 2027. Accrual accounting correctly matches performance to the exact period of economic activity.

Section 2.3

Qualitative Characteristics of Useful Financial Information (IFRS Conceptual Framework)

IFRS Standards
📌 TLDR — Section 2.3
For financial information to be useful, it must possess two Fundamental Qualities: Relevance (capable of making a difference through predictive/confirmatory value, subject to materiality) and Faithful Representation (completeness, neutrality/prudence, free from error). Its usefulness is enhanced by Comparability, Verifiability, Timeliness, and Understandability.
⭐ Fundamental Quality 1: Relevance

Capable of making a difference in user economic decisions. Key ingredients:

  • Predictive Value: Input for forecasting future operational outcomes.
  • Confirmatory Value: Feedback that confirms or alters previous user expectations.
  • Materiality: Entity-specific threshold. Information is material if omitting, misstating, or obscuring it could influence primary user decisions.
⭐ Fundamental Quality 2: Faithful Representation

Depicts the true economic substance of underlying transactions. Key ingredients:

  • Completeness: Includes all necessary descriptions, disclosures, and explanations.
  • Neutrality (Prudence): Free from bias in selection or presentation. Exercise caution under uncertainty.
  • Free from Error: No procedural errors or omissions in the measurement process (does not mean 100% predictive omniscience).
⚠️ The 6 Official Criteria for "Obscured Information" under Modern IFRS

Corporate executives cannot hide bad news behind impenetrable walls of jargon. Under PFRS, information is defined as obscured if presented in a manner producing a similar effect to omitting or misstating it:

  1. Material information is buried inside dense boilerplate legalese or vague technical language.
  2. An item of material information is scattered across disparate, unrelated footnotes.
  3. Dissimilar items are inappropriately aggregated together into a single vague line item (e.g., hiding a Php 50M government fine under "Office Supplies").
  4. Similar accounting items are unnecessarily fragmented across dozens of separate schedules to conceal total magnitude.
  5. Critical disclosures are camouflaged by overwhelming users with trivial, immaterial clutter.
  6. Ambiguous, confusing terminology is used that prevents readers from identifying true economic substance.
Section 2.4

The Four Enhancing Qualitative Characteristics

Value Amplifiers
1. Comparability

Enables users to identify similarities and differences across competing enterprises (cross-sectional) and across consecutive accounting periods (consistency over time). Changing accounting methods arbitrarily violates comparability.

2. Verifiability (Direct & Indirect)

Assures users that different knowledgeable, independent observers would reach consensus.
• Direct Verifiability: Physical observation (counting cash bills, counting inventory pallets).
• Indirect Verifiability: Recalculating mathematical inputs and formulas (verifying straight-line depreciation schedules or FIFO inventory math).

3. Timeliness

Having financial information available to decision-makers before it loses its capacity to influence resource allocation decisions. Older information is less useful.

4. Understandability

Classifying, characterizing, and presenting information clearly and concisely. Assumes users possess reasonable business and accounting literacy and study reports with diligence.

Section 2.5

General Accounting Principles & The Three Expense Recognition Modes

Operational Rules
1. Historical Cost Principle

Assets must be recorded at their original acquisition exchange price paid in an arm's-length cash transaction. Reliable and verifiable, protecting balance sheets from subjective executive hype.

2. Revenue Recognition Principle (PFRS 15)

Revenue is recognized when a promised performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of goods or services to the customer, regardless of cash receipt timing.

2.5.3 The Matching Principle & The Three Modes of Expense Recognition

Expenses must be matched against the specific revenues they helped produce in the exact same accounting period:

Mode A: Cause & Effect

Direct association between costs incurred and revenues generated. Examples: Sales commission paid to real estate agents; direct Cost of Goods Sold (COGS).

Mode B: Systematic Allocation

Spreading multi-period asset costs systematically across their estimated useful life. Examples: Straight-line depreciation of office equipment; monthly amortization of prepaid commercial rent.

Mode C: Immediate Recognition

Recognized as an expense immediately in the current period because no future economic benefit can be verified. Examples: Advertising campaigns, executive salaries, routine maintenance.

4. Full Disclosure Principle

Requires financial statements to disclose all material facts, accounting policies, debt covenants, and pending legal contingencies necessary for an informed evaluation. Accomplished through formal financial statements accompanied by transparent Notes to Financial Statements.

Section 2.6

Modifying Constraints & Foundational Doctrines

Practical Discretion
1. Materiality & Cost-Benefit

Departures from rigid GAAP are permissible if the amount is immaterial (e.g., expensing a Php 400 paper puncher immediately). The benefit of providing information must exceed the cost of compliance.

2. Conservatism / Prudence

When facing uncertain estimates, choose the alternative that is least likely to overstate assets and net income. Recognize probable losses immediately, but never anticipate unearned gains!

3. Substance Over Form

Economic reality takes precedence over strict legal technicalities. If a lease agreement is functionally an installment purchase, it must be recorded as an asset and debt on the balance sheet.

Section 2.7

Forensic Case Studies: When Accounting Principles Are Violated

Corporate Collapses
🚨 Wirecard AG (2020)

Fabricated €1.9 Billion (Php 110 Billion) in ghost cash supposedly deposited in Philippine escrow accounts at BDO and BPI.

Violations: Faithful Representation, Verifiability, and Objectivity. Disclosed assets that had zero existence in reality.

🚨 WorldCom (2002)

Fraudulently reclassified USD 3.8 Billion of routine network line access fees from operating expenses into capital asset accounts.

Violations: Matching Principle (Immediate Recognition) and Historical Cost. Inflated reported earnings and balance sheet assets.

🚨 Enron (2001)

Concealed billions in toxic debt using hundreds of off-balance-sheet Special Purpose Entities (SPEs) operated by its CFO.

Violations: Substance Over Form, Separate Entity, and Full Disclosure. Kept material liabilities off public view.

Section 2.8

🏛️ Departmental Exam Flashpoints: The Conceptual Traps & Doctrine Nuances

Exam High-Yield
📌 TLDR — Section 2.8
Departmental examinations for Unit 2 specifically test edge cases where general principles encounter boundary conditions. Master these four recurring high-yield distinctions from AY 2025–2026 exams:
1. Going Concern vs. Imminent Liquidation Exception

While the going concern assumption presumes an entity will operate indefinitely, imminent liquidation discards going concern.

The Departmental Trap (AY2526 T3): If a company faces severe legal battles pointing to liquidation within 5 months, the accountant cannot continue using historical cost under going concern. Assets must be written down to their net liquidation / realizable values.

2. Consistency vs. Uniformity

Under the qualitative characteristic of Comparability, consistency does NOT mean uniformity.

The Departmental Trap (AY2526 T2 & T3): Consistency is the application of the same accounting methods to the same items across periods within an entity. Uniformity (forcing unlike things to look identical) impairs faithful representation and is strictly rejected by the IFRS Conceptual Framework.

3. The Cost-Benefit Constraint

The reporting of financial information is constrained by practical economics: Benefits must justify costs.

The Departmental Trap (AY2526 T1 & T2): Companies are not required to report every microscopic transaction regardless of cost. If the administrative cost of compiling data exceeds its value to users, the information may be omitted under the cost-benefit constraint.

4. Accrual Revenue: Advances vs. Earned

Cash received prior to service delivery is a debt to the customer, not operational income.

The Departmental Trap (AY2526 T3): An accounting firm receiving a cash advance in November for services to be rendered in January must record an Unearned Service Revenue Liability in November. Crediting revenue or capital immediately is a direct violation of PFRS 15.

5. Direct vs. Indirect Verifiability

Verifiability assures users that independent observers could reach consensus.

Direct Verifiability: Verifying an amount through direct physical observation (e.g. counting cash bills or physical inventory boxes).
Indirect Verifiability: Checking the inputs into a model, formula, or technique and recalculating the outputs using the same methodology (e.g. verifying ending inventory via FIFO formula).

6. Subsequent Events (PAS 10) & Hyperinflation (PAS 29)

Specialized boundary standards frequently tested in advanced conceptual items.

PAS 10 (Non-Adjusting Events): A fire destroying a plant in January before the annual report is published is a non-adjusting event; disclose in the Notes without changing Dec 31 balance sheet figures.
PAS 29 (Hyperinflation): The stable monetary unit is abandoned when cumulative 3-year inflation approaches or exceeds 100%.

Section 3.1

The Financial Statement Architecture Under IFRS 18

Universal Standard
📌 TLDR — Section 3.1
Financial statements are an integrated package of structured reports showing an entity's financial position at a point in time (SFP) and performance over a period of time (SPL, SOE, SCF). In April 2024, the IASB issued IFRS 18 (replacing IAS 1) to enforce clearer categories, standardized operating profit subtotals, and more transparent disclosures.

Financial statements do not exist as isolated spreadsheets; they are a tightly interwoven mathematical tapestry:

Financial StatementPrimary Question AnsweredTime HorizonCore Mathematical Interconnection
1. Statement of Financial Position (SFP) What economic resources does the entity control and who holds claims against them? Point in time (Static Snapshot) Balances Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity utilizing ending capital from the SOE.
2. Statement of Profit or Loss (SPL) How profitable were operations over the artificial calendar interval? Period of time (Flow) Calculates Net Income = Revenues − Expenses, which flows directly into the SOE.
3. Statement of Changes in Equity (SOE) Why did owner's net worth increase or decrease over the period? Period of time (Reconciliation) Reconciles Ending Capital = Beg Capital + Investments + Net Income − Drawings.
4. Statement of Cash Flows (SCF) Where did physical cash come from and where was it disbursed? Period of time (Cash Inflows & Outflows) Reconciles starting cash to the exact ending Cash balance reported on the SFP.
5. Notes to Financial Statements What accounting policies, contingencies, and schedules explain the numbers? Accompanying Narrative Provides disaggregated schedules and accounting policies to achieve Full Disclosure.
Section 3.2

The Structural Anatomy of the Balance Sheet

Balance Sheet Trees
📌 TLDR — Section 3.2
The Balance Sheet is structured into three fundamental equations:
• Total Assets = Current Assets + Non-Current Assets
• Total Liabilities = Current Liabilities + Non-Current Liabilities
• Owner's Equity = Contributed Capital + Earned Capital − Owner's Withdrawals
1. Current Assets (Liquidity Order)

Economic resources expected to be converted to cash, sold, or consumed within 12 months or the operating cycle:

  • Cash & Cash Equivalents: Currency on hand, petty cash, bank deposits.
  • Trade Accounts Receivable: Unconditional claims against clients, less Allowance for Doubtful Accounts.
  • Short-Term Notes Receivable: Written promissory notes due within 1 yr.
  • Operating Supplies: Consumables on hand.
  • Prepaid Expenses: Rent or insurance paid in advance.
2. Non-Current Assets (PPE)

Productive tangible and intangible assets held for long-term operational use rather than immediate resale:

  • Land: Permanent operational property (does NOT depreciate).
  • Commercial Buildings: Reported at Cost less Accumulated Depreciation.
  • Office Equipment: Computers, desks, servers.
  • Contra-Asset Mechanism: Accumulated Depreciation carries a normal credit balance, offsetting asset cost to report net Carrying Value (Book Value).
3. Liabilities Architecture

Present obligations to transfer economic resources:

  • Current Liabilities: Due within 12 months (Accounts Payable, Unearned Service Fees, Salaries Payable, Utilities Payable, Short-term Notes).
  • Non-Current Liabilities: Long-term obligations maturing beyond 12 months (Mortgage Notes Payable secured by real estate, 5-year bank term loans).
Fundamental Accounting Equation
ASSETSCurrent + Non-Current
=
LIABILITIESCurrent + Non-Current
+
OWNER'S EQUITYContributed + Earned - Drawings
Section 3.2.4

Deferrals, Accruals, and Prepayments Master Framework

Timing & Classification
📌 TLDR — Section 3.2.4
Timing is the fundamental driver of financial statement classification. When the economic activity happens before cash changes hands, you have an Accrual (Accrued Income = Current Asset; Accrued Expense = Current Liability). When cash changes hands before the economic activity happens, you have a Deferral / Prepayment (Prepaid Expense = Current Asset; Unearned Income = Current Liability).
⚠️ Critical Pedagogical Scope Caveat (Subsequent Units Scope)
In Unit 3 (Financial Statements), our strict focus is on Statement of Financial Position (SFP) classification—identifying whether an item is a Current Asset or a Current Liability and understanding how it affects Working Capital and Total Assets. The multi-step mechanics of calculating period-end expirations and recording Adjusting Journal Entries (e.g., Asset Method vs. Expense Method for prepayments, Liability Method vs. Income Method for unearned revenues, and reversing entries) will be systematically mastered in subsequent units (specifically Unit 4: Adjusting Entries & The Complete Accounting Cycle).
Category Timing of Cash vs. Economic Event SFP Classification Standard Account Titles Departmental Exam Trap Alert
1. Accrued Income
(Accrued Revenue)		 Service earned / goods delivered FIRST; cash collected LATER. CURRENT ASSET Accrued Service Revenue, Accrued Interest Income, Accrued Rent Income Enforceable right to receive cash from clients; reported under Trade & Other Receivables.
2. Accrued Expense
(Accrued Payable)		 Economic benefit consumed FIRST; cash paid LATER. CURRENT LIABILITY Accrued Salaries Expense, Accrued Utilities Payable, Accrued Interest Payable Represents an unavoidable present obligation to transfer economic resources.
3. Prepaid Expense
(Deferred Expense / Prepayments)		 Cash paid FIRST in advance; benefit consumed LATER. CURRENT ASSET Prepaid Rent, Prepaid Insurance, Advances to Suppliers, Office Supplies Advances to Suppliers & Prepaid Expenses are Current Assets, NEVER operating expenses at time of payment!
4. Unearned Income
(Deferred Income)		 Cash collected FIRST in advance; service delivered LATER. CURRENT LIABILITY Unearned Service Revenue, Unearned Rent Income, Advances from Customers Advances from Customers & Unearned Fees are Current Liabilities (performance obligations), NEVER earned revenues!
🚨 Trap Alert: Advances to Employees

When a business advances money to an employee ahead of payroll, this is classified as a CURRENT ASSET (Receivable from Staff). It is not an expense until work is performed and payroll is settled.

🚨 Trap Alert: Advances from Customers

Cash collected from clients prior to performing the service is a CURRENT LIABILITY (Unearned Revenue). It represents a strict performance obligation to deliver service or refund cash.

Section 3.2.5

Master Computational Formulas & Balance Sheet Solving Guide

Exam Formula Bank
📌 TLDR — Section 3.2.5
Mastering financial statement arithmetic requires structural fluency in 8 core equations. Every problem-solving question in AY 2025–2026 departmental exams (including missing expenses, drawings, beginning capital, and ratio dynamics) is solvable using the systematic equations below.
1. Total Current Assets (TCA) Formula
TCA = Cash & Cash Equivalents
+ Accounts Receivable (net of Allowance)
+ Short-Term Notes Receivable (due ≤ 12 mos)
+ Interest Receivable
+ Merchandise Inventory / Supplies on Hand
+ Prepaid Expenses (Prepaid Rent, Insurance)
+ Accrued Income (Earned unbilled revenues)
+ Advances to Employees & Suppliers

⚠️ EXCLUSION RULE: Never include Office Equipment, Furniture, Delivery Vehicles, Land, Buildings, or Accumulated Depreciation in TCA!

2. Total Non-Current Assets (TNCA) & Cost Rule
TNCA = Land (Never depreciated)
+ Commercial Buildings − Accum. Depr.
+ Office Equipment − Accum. Depr.
+ Delivery Vehicles − Accum. Depr.
+ Furniture & Fixtures − Accum. Depr.
+ Long-Term Notes Receivable (> 12 mos)

📌 HISTORICAL COST PRINCIPLE: Land bought for Php 1.85M appraised at Php 3.7M is reported at Php 1.85M. Appraisals and buyer offers are strictly ignored!

3. Total Current Liabilities (TCL) Formula
TCL = Trade Accounts Payable
+ Short-Term Notes Payable (due ≤ 12 mos)
+ Accrued Expenses (Salaries, Utilities, Interest)
+ Unearned Revenues (Fees, Rent Income)
+ Advances from Customers
+ Bank Overdrafts

Total Liabilities (TL) = Total Current Liabilities + Long-Term Notes Payable + Mortgage Payable.

4. Working Capital & Current Ratio Dynamics
Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities

• When CR > 1.0: Paying CL with cash increases Current Ratio. Buying inventory on credit decreases Current Ratio.
• When CR < 1.0: Paying CL with cash decreases Current Ratio.

🧮 5. Owner's Equity Reconciliation & Missing Variable Solvers (Item 125 Master Formula)
Master Reconciliation Equation: Ending Equity = Beginning Equity + Additional Investments + (Revenues − Expenses) − Drawings
Target Missing VariableDerived Mathematical FormulaApplication to AY 2025–2026 Exam Questions
Solving for Total Expenses
(Item 125 Pattern)		 Expenses = Revenues − Net Income
where Net Income = Ending Equity − Beg Equity − Inv + Drawings		 Example (Item 125): Initial Inv = Php 120k, Drawings = Php 100k, Ending Equity = Php 140k, Revenues = Php 800k.
1. Net Income = Php 140,000 − Php 120,000 + Php 100,000 = Php 120,000.
2. Total Expenses = Php 800,000 − Php 120,000 = Php 680,000.
Solving for Owner's Drawings Drawings = Beg Equity + Investments + Net Income − Ending Equity Reverses the equity equation when owner neglected to report personal withdrawals.
Solving for Beginning Equity Beg Equity = Ending Equity − Investments − Net Income + Drawings Reconstructs starting net worth from ending balance sheet and performance reports.
Ratio Multipliers If Liabilities = 40% of Assets → Equity = 60% of Assets → Assets = Equity / 0.60.
If Equity = 1/3 of Assets → Liabilities = 2/3 of Assets (or 2 × Equity).		 Solves dual-variable questions where one element is expressed as a ratio of total assets.
Accrual Service Revenue Revenues = Cash Collected for Current Period + Uncollected Billed AR Excludes advance customer payments (unearned liabilities) from earned revenue.
Section 3.3

The Capital Concept: Accounting Net Worth vs. Finance Total Capital Employed

Interdisciplinary Nuance
📌 TLDR — Section 3.3
In Accounting, "Capital" refers strictly to Owner's Equity (Assets − Liabilities). In Finance, "Capital" refers to Total Invested Capital (Debt + Equity). While accountants focus on residual net worth for legal stewardship, finance executives focus on the total pool of funding needed to buy operating assets and calculate the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).
In Financial Accounting

Capital = Owner's Equity = Assets − Liabilities

Represents the net residual wealth contributed and accumulated by the proprietors. Third-party bank loans are debts owed to outsiders, not capital.

In Corporate Finance

Invested Capital = Debt Capital + Equity Capital

Represents the entire pool of funding utilized to acquire operating assets. Finance evaluates the capital structure to determine financial leverage risk and optimize the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).

Section 3.4

SFP Formats & Statement of Profit or Loss (SPL)

Presentation Models
Report Form SFP

Presents Assets, Liabilities, and Owner's Equity in a single continuous vertical column sequence. Standard in published corporate annual reports due to vertical page reading layout.

Account Form SFP

Presents Assets on the left side and Liabilities & Owner's Equity on the right side, visually mirroring the classical two-sided T-account format.

3.4.3 Statement of Profit or Loss: Natural Format for Service Entities

Under IFRS 18, service entities present operating expenses categorized by their nature (Natural Format):

Line ItemClassificationDescription
Service RevenuesOperating InflowTotal fees billed and earned from clients during the period.
Salaries & Wages ExpenseOperating ExpenseCompensation paid and accrued to personnel for service delivery.
Rent ExpenseOperating ExpenseCommercial office space consumed during the period.
Utilities ExpenseOperating ExpenseElectricity, water, and internet consumed.
Depreciation ExpenseOperating Expense (Non-cash)Systematic allocation of equipment cost over its useful life.
Supplies ExpenseOperating ExpenseConsumables used during the period (Beginning + Purchases - Ending).
NET INCOME / (LOSS)Bottom-Line PerformanceRevenues − Total Expenses. Flows directly into the SOE!
⚠️ Critical Distinction: Why Accounting Profit Does NOT Equal Cash Flow
  1. Credit Sales: Billed services generate revenue immediately on the SPL today, but cash may not be collected for 30–60 days.
  2. Non-Cash Expenses: Depreciation reduces reported net income, but no physical cash leaves the bank account when recording it.
  3. Advance Payments & Capex: Buying a delivery van for Php 1,500,000 drains cash today, but does not appear on the income statement as an expense (it is capitalized as an asset).
  4. Owner's Drawings: Cash taken out by owners for personal groceries drains cash immediately, but is an equity distribution, never an SPL operating expense!

Section 3.6

Statement of Cash Flows (Direct Method Mechanics)

Liquidity Lifeblood
📌 TLDR — Section 3.6
The Statement of Cash Flows (SCF) classifies physical cash movements into three operational categories: 1. Operating Activities: Daily commercial trading engine (cash collected from clients less cash paid to suppliers, staff, and BIR). 2. Investing Activities: Capital investments in long-term infrastructure (buying/selling PPE). 3. Financing Activities: Transactions with debt and equity capital providers (owner investments, owner drawings, bank borrowings, loan principal repayments).
1. Operating Activities

+ Cash collections from customers
- Cash paid to suppliers for goods/services
- Cash paid to employees for wages
- Cash paid for utilities and taxes

2. Investing Activities

- Cash paid to purchase office equipment
- Cash paid to purchase commercial delivery vans
+ Cash proceeds from sale of used equipment

3. Financing Activities

+ Cash investment from owner
+ Cash proceeds from bank loan
- Cash withdrawals by owner for personal use
- Cash paid for bank loan principal

Section 3.7

🏛️ Departmental Exam Flashpoints: SFP Formats, Classification Traps & Equation Solvers

Exam Master Key
📌 TLDR — Section 3.7
The Departmental Examination for Unit 3 heavily features two presentation styles, five account classification traps, and mathematical algebraic reconciliations. Master these verified patterns from AY 2025–2026 exams:
1. Account Form vs. Report Form

Account Form (Horizontal): Follows a T-account structure. Assets are listed on the left, while Liabilities and Owner's Equity are listed on the right.

Report Form (Vertical): All sections are presented vertically in a single downward cascade (Assets on top, followed by Liabilities and Equity below).

2. Account Classification Traps
  • Advances to Employees: CURRENT ASSET (Receivable from staff, not an expense).
  • Accrued Revenue / Commissions: CURRENT ASSET (Earned, unbilled asset).
  • Unearned Fees / Rent: CURRENT LIABILITY (Cash collected in advance of performance).
  • Accrued Salaries / Rent: CURRENT LIABILITY (Consumed, unpaid obligation).
  • Furniture / Vehicles / Equipment: NON-CURRENT PPE ASSET (Never expensed immediately!).
3. Missing Variable Solvers

Solving for Missing Drawings:

Drawings = Beg Cap + Add'l Inv + Net Income − End Cap

Solving for Missing Beg Capital:

Beg Cap = End Cap − Add'l Inv − Net Income + Drawings

Ratio Multipliers: If Equity = 1/3 Assets → Liabilities = 2/3 Assets (or 2 × Equity). If Liabilities = 2 × Equity → Assets = 3 × Equity.

4. Current Ratio Dynamics (Counter-Intuitive Math)

When Current Ratio > 1.0: Paying current liabilities in cash increases the Current Ratio. Buying inventory on credit decreases it.

When Current Ratio < 1.0: Paying current liabilities in cash decreases the Current Ratio further!

Collecting Accounts Receivable: Zero effect on Working Capital or Current Ratio (exchanges one current asset for another).

5. Cash Flow & Operating Cycle Rules

Operating Cycle Exception: Assets realized within the normal operating cycle (e.g. 18-month aging wine, real estate construction) qualify as Current Assets even if exceeding 12 months.

Non-Cash Investing/Financing: Transactions not requiring cash (e.g. buying a building with a mortgage, owner contributing equipment) are excluded from the Statement of Cash Flows and disclosed in the Notes.

6. Notes to Financial Statements Sequence

Note 1 (Corporate Info): Domicile, legal form, country of incorporation, and description of principal operations.

Note 2 (Accounting Policies): Measurement bases (historical cost vs fair value), depreciation formulas, and revenue recognition policies under PFRS.

Empirical Research Gateway

Publicly Listed Company Filings & Audited Financial Statements (AFS)

SEC & PSE EDGE

Under Philippine law and IFRS, publicly traded corporations must upload audited periodic reports for public inspection. As accounting and finance students at DLSU, you are expected to analyze real-world Audited Financial Statements directly from primary regulatory repositories:

🇵🇭 PSE EDGE (Electronic Disclosure Generation Technology)
https://edge.pse.com.ph

The official disclosure system of the Philippine Stock Exchange. Search any listed company ticker (e.g., BDO, ALI, SMPH, GLO, TEL, AC) to access SEC Form 17-A (Annual Reports) with full Notes to Financial Statements and Independent Auditor Reports.
🏛️ SEC eFAST (Electronic Filing and Submission Tool)
https://efast.sec.gov.ph

The central corporate filing registry of the Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission. Contains official AFS filings, General Information Sheets (GIS), and corporate articles of both public corporations and private enterprises in the Philippines.

4.1 Anatomy of a Philippine Annual Report (SEC Form 17-A)

When downloading an audited report from PSE EDGE, the document is organized into standard regulatory sections:

Report SectionContents & FocusAudit Relevance
Independent Auditor's Report The official audit opinion signed by the CPA firm (SGV, PwC Isla Lipana, KPMG R.G. Manabat, Deloitte Navarro Amper). Look for an Unmodified (Clean) Opinion stating the financial statements "present fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with PFRS."
Financial Statements Suite Statement of Financial Position, Statement of Profit or Loss, Statement of Comprehensive Income, Statement of Changes in Equity, Statement of Cash Flows. Presents comparative columns (current year vs. prior year) to satisfy the Comparability qualitative characteristic.
Notes to Financial Statements Note 1 (Corporate Information), Note 2 (Summary of Significant Accounting Policies), followed by detailed breakdowns of cash, receivables, debt maturities, and contingencies. Provides disaggregated information required by the Full Disclosure Principle. Over 80% of an AFS's volume consists of Notes!

Question 1 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 5 pts History Matching

1.1 Brief History of Accounting: Match each historical accounting milestone to its corresponding civilization, period, or figure:

Some scholars claim that account records date back to the ___________ keeping track of crop and herd growth.
During the ___________ period, with international trade flourishing...
...with international trade flourishing, the ___________ started documenting various expeditions and shipment of goods.
A monk and a mathematician, ___________, who also happens to be a friend of Leonardo da Vinci...
...published the first known description of the ___________ of bookkeeping entitled Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et Proportionalite in 1494.
Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Question 2 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

Bookkeeping and accounting are one and the same because the bookkeeping function includes the accounting process.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Bookkeeping is the clerical/mechanical recording phase of accounting transactions. Accounting is a much broader analytical discipline encompassing designing information systems, classifying, summarizing, analyzing, auditing, and interpreting financial reports.
Question 3 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

The primary role of accounting is to determine the amount of taxes a business will be required to pay to taxing entities.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. The primary role of accounting is to provide relevant, faithfully represented financial information about economic resources and claims to assist stakeholders in making sound economic decisions. Tax determination is merely one specialized branch/function.
Question 4 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

Accounting is thought to be the 'language of business' because business information is communicated to stakeholders.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Accounting translates diverse physical commercial operations (sales, hiring, borrowing, manufacturing) into standardized financial terms understood by investors, lenders, regulators, and managers globally.
Question 5 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

Managerial accounting information is used by external and internal users equally.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Managerial accounting is prepared strictly for internal users (management, executives) for operational planning, budgeting, cost control, and decision-making. External users rely on general-purpose Financial Accounting.
Question 6 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

Financial accounting provides information to all of the business stakeholders, while the main focus for managerial accounting is to provide information to the management.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Financial accounting generates general-purpose financial statements for external stakeholders (investors, creditors) and general users, whereas managerial accounting produces confidential internal reports tailored for executive decision-making.
Question 7 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

Accounting Information System deals with helping clients to improve their information system and business performance.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Helping external clients improve systems and performance is the function of Management Advisory Services (MAS) / Consulting. Accounting Information Systems (AIS) is the internal structure used to collect, store, manage, and process accounting data.
Question 8 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Which of the following best describes accounting?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Accounting is an information system that identifies, measures, records, and communicates economic information about an organization to interested stakeholders.
Question 9 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Which of the following is NOT a role of accounting in business?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Accountants do not personally guarantee corporate loans! The role of accounting is informational and analytical—providing data for management and stakeholders.
Question 10 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Tax accountants would be responsible for providing the following information:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Tax accounting specializes in tax compliance (calculating liability and filing tax returns to the BIR) and tax planning (legally structuring transactions to minimize taxes).
Question 11 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Deals with the review of financial statements to assess their fairness and adherence to accounting principles:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Auditing (specifically external auditing) is the independent examination of financial statements by a CPA to express an opinion on whether they present fairly in accordance with PFRS/GAAP.
Question 12 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

The rights or claims to the assets of a business may be subdivided into rights of creditors and rights of owners thus making creditors and investors the primary users of financial statements.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Total assets are claimed by creditors (Liabilities) and owners (Equity). Under IFRS Conceptual Framework Section 1.5, existing and potential investors, lenders, and other creditors are the Primary Users.
Question 13 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

Primary users of accounting information are accountants.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Accountants are the preparers and auditors of accounting information. The primary users are external resource providers: existing and potential investors, lenders, and creditors.
Question 14 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Concept T/F

An example of a business stakeholder is the government.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Government agencies (such as the BIR, SEC, and DOLE) are stakeholders who rely on accounting data for tax collection, statutory regulation, and economic statistics.
Question 15 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

The following are examples of internal users of financial statements EXCEPT:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Financial analysts are external users who analyze public financial statements on behalf of investing clients. Managers, owners (in owner-managed firms), and employees are internal stakeholders.
Question 16 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

A regulatory agency that oversees the financial information provided by publicly listed companies in the Philippines:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
The Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulates corporations and publicly listed companies, mandating annual AFS filings (SEC Form 17-A) and quarterly reports (SEC Form 17-Q).
Question 17 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Which of the following statements is TRUE?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
A corporation is an artificial being created by operation of law, possessing a legal personality separate and distinct from its shareholders (Revised Corporation Code RA 11232).
Question 18 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Most businesses in the economy are organized as:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Sole proprietorships are numerically the most common form of business organization due to low startup costs and ease of formation.
Question 19 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Which of the items below is NOT a recognized legal business organization form?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Entrepreneurship is a process, economic activity, or academic mindset—it is not a recognized legal form of business organization under Philippine law.
Question 20 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

The following are components of the definition of a partnership, EXCEPT:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Under Article 1799 of the Civil Code of the Philippines, any stipulation excluding one or more partners from any share in profits or losses is strictly VOID (pactum leoninum).
Question 21 • Unit 1 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Which of the following is FALSE about a manufacturing business?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Manufacturing businesses can be micro, small, or large (e.g., a neighborhood panaderia, craft brewery, or furniture carpenter converts raw materials into finished goods and is a manufacturer).
Question 1 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Conceptual T/F

The two fundamental qualitative characteristics that make accounting information useful for decision-making by interested users are predictive value and confirmatory value.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. The two fundamental qualitative characteristics are Relevance and Faithful Representation. Predictive value and confirmatory value are ingredients of Relevance.
Question 2 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Conceptual T/F

In order for accounting information to be relevant in making a difference in decision-making, it must have predictive value, confirmatory value, or both, and also must be free from error to be relevant.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Free from error is an ingredient of Faithful Representation, not Relevance. Relevance requires predictive value, confirmatory value, and materiality.
Question 3 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

A fundamental qualitative characteristic that ensures that accounting information is presented without bias in the selection or presentation of financial information:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Neutrality (supported by prudence) requires that financial statements are prepared without bias in selection or presentation to avoid slanting user perceptions.
Question 4 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

When there is an agreement between a measure or description and the phenomenon it purports to represent, relevant information possesses which quality?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Faithful representation means financial reports correspond to and accurately reflect the true economic substance of underlying transactions.
Question 5 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

The following are attributes that enhance the relevance and faithful representation of financial information, EXCEPT:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Materiality is an entity-specific aspect of Relevance (a fundamental quality). The four Enhancing Qualities are Comparability, Verifiability, Timeliness, and Understandability.
Question 6 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Generally accepted accounting principles are:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
GAAP (and PFRS/IFRS) are professional standards and conventions establishing how economic events must be measured, recognized, presented, and disclosed.
Question 7 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Assumption T/F

An organization for accounting purposes, stands apart from other organizations and individuals as a separate accounting entity.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Under the Business / Separate Entity assumption, the accounting records of the entity must be maintained completely separate from its owners and other firms.
Question 8 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

The business entity concept means that:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
The business is treated as an independent economic unit. The owner's personal living expenditures must never be commingled with company operating expenses.
Question 9 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Assumption T/F

The going-concern principle states an entity will remain in operation for only the next accounting period.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Going concern assumes the business will operate indefinitely into the foreseeable future (not just for one period), justifying carrying assets at historical cost less depreciation.
Question 10 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

A problem with the monetary unit assumption is that:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
The monetary unit assumption assumes the currency has stable purchasing power. In reality, general economic inflation erodes the peso's value over decades.
Question 11 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the monetary unit assumption?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Standard historical cost accounting assumes the purchasing power of the currency remains stable over time for ordinary reporting, ignoring everyday price fluctuations.
Question 12 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Assumption T/F

The Time Period Assumption requires that all business transactions must occur within the same accounting period.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Transactions occur continuously throughout the life of the enterprise. The Time Period assumption artificially subdivides that continuous operating life into equal calendar intervals (months, quarters, years).
Question 13 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

The Time Period Assumption is most essential for which financial statement?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
The Statement of Profit or Loss measures operating performance and profitability over a defined artificial time interval (e.g., 'For the Year Ended December 31, 2026').
Question 14 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Assumption T/F

Under the Accrual Assumption, revenue is recognized before cash is received, as long as it is earned; while expense is recognized before cash is paid, as long as it is incurred.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Accrual basis dictates that economic events are recognized when they occur (earned or incurred), regardless of the timing of cash receipts or disbursements.
Question 15 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Multiple Choice

The Accrual Assumption in accounting dictates that:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Revenues are recorded when earned (performance obligation satisfied) and expenses when incurred (consumed), matching economic activity to the appropriate period.
Question 16 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Principle MCQ

The historical cost principle requires that when assets are acquired, they be recorded at:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Historical cost is the cash or cash equivalent exchange price paid to acquire an asset in an arm's-length transaction, providing verifiable and objective evidence.
Question 17 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Principle MCQ

The relevant measure of value of the assets of a company that is going out of business is their:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
When the going concern assumption no longer holds (company facing bankruptcy or liquidation), assets must be written down to their net realizable / fire-sale liquidation value.
Question 18 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Principle T/F

Services or goods delivered in 2023 but collected in 2024 should be recognized as income in 2023.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Under the revenue recognition principle and accrual basis, revenue is recognized when the performance obligation is completed (goods delivered/services rendered in 2023).
Question 19 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Principle MCQ

A referral fee was given to a doctor for bringing his patients for laboratory exams at A1 Laboratory. Referral Expenses and Laboratory Expenses are recorded by A1 Laboratory against the service fees earned for the period. The method of recording expenses and revenue supports the principle of:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
The Matching Principle (Cause and Effect mode) requires that costs directly incurred to generate specific revenues (such as referral fees paid to doctors) be recognized in the same period as the revenue.
Question 20 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Principle MCQ

What is the primary objective of full disclosure in financial reporting?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Full disclosure ensures all material financial facts and contingencies are clearly communicated in the financial statements and accompanying notes so users are not misled.
Question 21 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Constraint MCQ

A deviation from generally accepted accounting principles is:

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Under the Materiality Constraint, companies may depart from strict GAAP for items so trivial that their omission or misstatement would not influence user decisions (e.g. immediately expensing a Php 300 stapler).
Question 22 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Constraint MCQ

The cost-benefit constraint goes hand in hand with which principle?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
The cost-benefit constraint and materiality are closely coupled: the cost of gathering, tracking, and depreciating immaterial items far outweighs any analytical benefit to financial users.
Question 23 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Constraint T/F

The cost-benefit test constraint refers to the benefit of complying with an accounting principle should not outweigh the cost of compliance.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Phrasing trap! The cost-benefit constraint requires that the benefits derived from providing financial information should exceed (outweigh) the costs incurred to provide it.
Question 24 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Constraint T/F

With Conservatism, if an accountant has more than one Generally Accepted Accounting Principles options to choose from when facing an accounting challenge, the one that yields inferior numbers should be selected.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Conservatism (prudence) directs the accountant, when facing equally valid estimates, to choose the alternative that is least likely to overstate assets and income, resulting in the more conservative ('inferior') numerical valuation.
Question 25 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Constraint MCQ

It is usually the case that industry practice becomes acceptable as GAAP in what types of industries?

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Specialized industry practices are recognized as GAAP where unique operating conditions, severe risks, or statutory regulatory frameworks exist (such as banking, public utilities, agriculture, and mining).
Question 26 • Unit 2 Canvas Quiz • 10 pts Application Matrix (10 pts)

Application of Accounting Concepts: Match the accounting concept, principle, assumption, or constraint applicable in each of the 10 real-world business scenarios:

1. Expenses incurred amounting to Php 20,000 are offset against revenue of Php 25,000 earned in the same period.
2. A company owns land that cost Php 5M with a fair value of Php 6.5M. The firm continues to report the asset on the Statement of Financial Position at Php 5M.
3. A large company purchases a Php 500 calculator and expensed it immediately instead of recording it as an asset and depreciating it over its useful life.
4. A loss of Php 20,000 is estimated and is highly probable to occur. This loss is shown in the Statement of Profit or Loss.
5. The financial performance of a company is measured every end of the month.
6. A statement of account is received from PLDT for communication services. This bill is recorded as expense although payment is to be made the next accounting period.
7. A company rendered various services amounting to Php 30,000 in December. The company's credit terms require the customer to pay within 45 days. The company's Statement of Profit or Loss reported the revenue in December.
8. The financial statements include notes to financial statements which show breakdown of aggregated amounts.
9. The mining industry uses the double declining balance method in accounting for depreciation although the Bureau of Internal Revenue generally requires straight line method.
10. A business owner paid the electricity bill for his house and the cash was taken from the business bank account. This was recorded as an owner’s drawings instead of expenses of the business.
Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
Question 1 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

Financial statements provide information about business activities to decision-makers.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Financial statements are general-purpose structured summaries conveying economic resources, claims, and operating performance to assist external and internal users in making resource allocation decisions.
Question 2 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

The Statement of Financial Position lists all the entity's assets, liabilities, and owner's equity as of a specific date.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. The Statement of Financial Position (Balance Sheet) is a snapshot of financial condition at a single moment in time (e.g., 'As of December 31, 2026').
Question 3 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

In order to possess future service potential, an asset must have physical substance.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Many valuable assets lack physical substance, such as Accounts Receivable, Notes Receivable, Copyrights, Patents, Franchises, and Software Licenses (Intangible Assets).
Question 4 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

Owner’s equity is often referred to as capital and represents the residual amount of business assets that can be claimed by the owner.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Under the IFRS Conceptual Framework, Equity is defined as the residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting all its liabilities (Assets − ext{Liabilities} = ext{Owner's Equity}).
Question 5 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

The basic accounting equation is in balance when the creditor and ownership claims against the business equal the assets.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Total Assets = Creditor Claims (Liabilities) + Ownership Claims (Owner's Equity). Economic resources equal the claims against those resources.
Question 6 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

A Statement of Profit or Loss is dated for a period of time such as 'Year Ended December 31, 2023.'

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Unlike the balance sheet which is a static point-in-time snapshot, the income statement (SPL) measures operational performance over a period of time.
Question 7 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

The Statement of Profit or Loss must be prepared before the Statement of Owner’s Equity.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. Net Income (or Net Loss) calculated on the Statement of Profit or Loss is a direct mathematical input required to determine Ending Capital on the Statement of Changes in Owner's Equity.
Question 8 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

The Statement of Cash Flows shows how much the cash account either increased or decreased.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
True. The Statement of Cash Flows details all cash inflows and outflows across Operating, Investing, and Financing activities to reconcile the net change in the Cash account.
Question 9 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

Net income for the period is determined by subtracting total expenses and drawings from total revenues.

Official Answer Key & Pedagogical Guidance:
False. Net Income is strictly Revenues − Expenses. Owner's Drawings are personal distributions of capital, reported on the Statement of Changes in Owner's Equity, NOT an operating expense on the SPL!
Question 10 • Unit 3 Canvas Quiz • 1 pt Statement T/F

In the Statement of Owner’s Equity, revenues are listed first, followed by expenses.
